name: Electron
price_source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rocket_Lab_Electron ("About US$7.5 million", citing Bloomberg, 3 Feb 2020, and The Washington Post, 2 Oct 2020)
description: A small rocket, 18 m tall. You buy the whole launch, so it takes your spacecraft to the orbit you choose.
why_it_matters: A rocket of your own goes where and when you want. You pay for the whole rocket even if your spacecraft is tiny.
source: Electron Payload User Guide v7.0 (1 Nov 2022), https://rocketlabcorp.com/assets/Electron-Payload-User-Guide-7.0-v6.pdf
estimate_basis: The guide states 200 kg to a 500 km sun-synchronous orbit. The other three capacities are read from the performance chart on page 35 of the guide (about 2 kg reading error) and rounded down to the nearest 5 kg. The 400 km, 51.6 degree value is interpolated between the 40 and 60 degree curves.
notes: The launch record includes HASTE suborbital flights of the same rocket. The 4 non-successes are failures. The price is from 2020 press reports.

name: Falcon 9 rideshare
description: A place on a large rocket shared with many other small satellites. It is cheap, but it flies to one orbit only.
why_it_matters: Sharing a rocket cuts the launch price a lot. In return you take the orbit and the launch date the main flight gives you.
source: SpaceX Rideshare Payload User's Guide v11, https://storage.googleapis.com/rideshare-static/Rideshare_Payload_Users_Guide.pdf
estimate_basis: Price: US$350,000 for up to 50 kg to sun-synchronous orbit plus US$7,000 per extra kilogram, taken from a secondary source because SpaceX's own price page could not be read. Capacity: SpaceX publishes no mass limit per payload; 450 kg is a working cap for the game, taken from the top bracket of the guide's load table ("451 kg +"). Orbits other than sun-synchronous are sold by quote only, so they are marked as not served.
notes: The fairing size is the whole Falcon 9 fairing (from the Wikipedia Falcon 9 page), which rideshare payloads share. The record counts 2 failures and 1 partial failure as non-successes.

name: Alpha
price_source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Firefly_Alpha ("US$15-17.6 million", citing a Firefly press release, 5 Oct 2022)
description: A rocket about 29 m tall that carries roughly three times as much as Electron. You buy the whole launch.
why_it_matters: More lifting power leaves room for a heavier spacecraft. It costs more, and a newer rocket has a shorter track record.
estimate_basis: The guide states 630 kg to a 500 km sun-synchronous orbit. The other three capacities are read from the guide's performance charts (about 5 kg reading error) and rounded down to the nearest 10 kg. The 400 km, 51.6 degree value is interpolated between the 50 and 62 degree curves. Price: the published range is US$15 to 17.6 million; the lower figure is used.
notes: The 4 non-successes are 2 failures and 2 partial failures. The last flight listed was on 12 Mar 2026.
